source_read: PMC HTML, PMC5419581 (author manuscript): abstract, all body sections, Figure 1-4 legends, acknowledgments/funding and reference list read in full; Figure 2 forest plot read on the rendered image. Supplementary material (docx) not opened (download).

claims.overstatement: Minor population mismatch: the pooled g = -1.47 is for 'amphetamine-like stimulant users' and the 9-study pool includes one study of recreational dexamphetamine users (Schouw et al., 2013), so it is not purely 'adults with a history of heavy methamphetamine use'. The magnitude field words this correctly ('amphetamine-type stimulant users'); the statement could say 'methamphetamine or amphetamine'.
claims.note: All pooled numbers match: g -1.47 (95% CI -1.83 to -1.10), 9 studies, 108 users, 126 controls, p<0.001. The 20-28% individual-study figures and the overlap of individual values come from other sources; this meta-analysis gives no individual-level data. The source supports the claim's closing sentence (temporal relationship and pre-existing differences unresolved).

anchors.extracted: 9 studies of amphetamine-like stimulant users (refs 27-35), 108 users vs 126 controls: pooled random-effects effect size -1.47 (95% CI -1.83 to -1.1), p<0.001. All 12 stimulant DAT studies combined (3 cocaine): 177 users vs 191 controls, g -0.91 (95% CI -1.5 to -0.32), p<0.01; cocaine studies inconsistent (two SPECT studies elevated, two PET no difference).

Individual study SMDs in the 9-study pool range from -0.82 (McCann 2008, 95% CI -1.74 to 0.10) to -2.25 (Yuan 2014); 2 of 9 CIs include zero (McCann 2008; Schouw 2013, recreational dexamphetamine users, -0.94, -1.92 to 0.04). RE model -1.47 (-1.83 to -1.10).

Abstinence in most included studies 5 days to 3 weeks; studies vary in abstinence duration, comorbid nicotine/alcohol use, radiotracer and striatal delineation; heterogeneity low except for the dopamine transporter analyses; few large studies (funnel plots).

anchors.locator: Discussion > Implications for understanding stimulant misuse and dependence, paras 3-7
anchors.extracted: Authors give competing explanations for lower DAT: loss of neurons or terminal damage, adaptive down-regulation (compensatory), or reductions that precede use (genetic/environmental risk), and state that current findings do not address the temporal relationship; longitudinal studies needed.

claims.note: This source only touches the claim's direction-by-abstinence pattern: elevated VMAT2 binding in two early-abstinence studies and lower binding in one PET study after longer abstinence. It gives no percentages (not the 28% or the ~10%), no post-mortem VMAT2 data and none of the Boileau 2016 BPND values; those must come from other sources. Note its abstinence label for the low-VMAT2 study is 'three months' (Johanson 2006), which the claim calls 'long-abstinent'. Ashok's own caveat runs the other way from Boileau's: residual methamphetamine competing at the tracer site could make VMAT2 underestimated.

anchors.extracted: Four VMAT2 studies, inconsistent: lower VMAT2 in cocaine users after ~2 weeks (Narendran 2012) and in methamphetamine users after ~3 months of abstinence (Johanson 2006; g printed as +1.68, 95% CI 0.86 to 2.5, though described as a reduction); higher VMAT2 in two recently abstinent methamphetamine samples (mean abstinence 2.6 and 19 days; Boileau 2008, 2016), pooled g 1.16 (0.56 to 1.76). Authors caution residual drug at the tracer site may lead to underestimated VMAT2.

claims.note: Consistent with the claim's 'not established' framing. The source also leans the other way in places: it cites two epidemiological studies (Callaghan 2012; Curtin 2015) as preliminary evidence that use might accelerate age-related dopamine neuron degeneration in some cases, and it notes that release and D2/3 reductions persisted after ~9 months of abstinence in one study while DAT recovered. The Parkinson's-pattern comparison in the claim comes from other sources.

anchors.locator: Discussion > Implications for understanding stimulant misuse and dependence, para 3
anchors.extracted: Lower release and DAT in amphetamine-type users could reflect neuron loss or terminal damage; but human DAT recovers with detoxification (interpreted as no neuron loss), the only post-mortem study (Wilson 1996) found lower DAT without dopamine neuron loss, and two epidemiological studies of Parkinson's disease risk are called preliminary evidence that use might accelerate age-associated degeneration in some cases.

Alternative models (tolerance/adaptive down-regulation; pre-existing reductions; hybrid); reductions in release and D2/3 reported after ~9 months of abstinence (Volkow 2015); temporal relationship not addressed by current data.

key_findings.correction: Content confirmed, but the statement that the data cannot address the temporal relationship is in the 8th paragraph of Discussion > Implications for understanding stimulant misuse and dependence ('This highlights one fundamental issue...'). Locator should read 3rd-8th paragraphs.

Arithmetic confirmed (19+12=31; 342+177=519; 321+191=512; release refs 16-22 all fall inside the D2/3 set). But not all VMAT2 studies are outside the count: Johanson 2006 (ref 28), one of the four VMAT2 studies, is counted in the DAT set. The DOPA study (ref 49), the D1 study (ref 53) and the other three VMAT2 studies (refs 50-52) are outside it.

reporting_issues.note: Also visible on the rendered Figure 2: the -0.91 (-1.50 to -0.32) is the 'Over all RE Model' row that includes the three cocaine studies; the amphetamine/methamphetamine RE row is -1.47 (-1.83 to -1.10).
The -0.81 point estimate matches the amphetamine-type D2/3 estimate, but its interval (-1.34 to -0.29) does not; -0.71 (-0.91 to -0.52) matches nothing.

The review never says VMAT2 studies were too few to pool; it says 'too few' only for amphetamine-type release studies and for cocaine DAT studies, and describes VMAT2 findings as inconsistent. The substantive issue stands: one g (1.16, 0.56 to 1.76) is given for two studies with no pooling method described. Cross-check: 1.16 (0.56 to 1.76) is exactly the Hedges' g I compute for Boileau 2016 alone (scan 1, whole striatum, 3.09 +/- 0.71, n=28 vs 2.41 +/- 0.34, n=22), so the figure attributed to 'two studies' appears to be the single 2016 study, not a pooled estimate.
Ref 37 is Volkow et al. 1997 (cocaine uptake in detoxified users); ref 54 is Volkow et al. 1997 (subjective effects and DAT occupancy).
The same wording is also in the Figure 1 legend.

risk_of_bias.note: AMSTAR 2 critically low agreed: no protocol, no risk-of-bias appraisal of primary studies, combined DAT estimate pools opposite-direction cocaine studies (+0.70, +0.75, +0.07 on Figure 2) with amphetamine-type studies, publication-bias results not discussed. The domain 11 note can now cite Figure 2 directly.

interpretation_gap.note: 'Substantial' agreed: abstract and Conclusions say 'down-regulated' and 'robust' while the Discussion's own models paragraphs and paragraph 8 concede that the data cannot address timing or mechanism.

missed: Figure 2 (rendered image) is readable and gives the individual study estimates the card says were not extracted: amphetamine-type SMDs range from -0.82 (McCann 2008, 95% CI -1.74 to 0.10) to -2.25 (Yuan 2014, -2.96 to -1.54); 2 of 9 intervals include zero (McCann 2008; Schouw 2013, recreational dexamphetamine users, -0.94, -1.92 to 0.04); cocaine studies +0.70, +0.75 and +0.07.

Discussion > Implications, paragraph 7: the authors state that receptor density and release remained lower even after about 9 months of abstinence (citing Volkow 2015), while DAT recovered. Relevant to the 'some markers return toward normal' part of cl_meth_dopamine_damage and not recorded on the card.

Results > Other dopaminergic measures: the authors' caveat (residual methamphetamine at the tracer site could make VMAT2 underestimated) runs in the opposite direction from Boileau's interpretation of elevated early-abstinence VMAT2 binding (less competition from depleted vesicular dopamine); worth flagging where the two sources are cited together for cl_meth_vmat2.

Minor: the 'Clinical implications' section repeats two sentences verbatim (D2/3 receptors 'stand out' and the relapse-prediction sentence), an editing duplication in the author manuscript; no consequence for the data.

The VMAT2 g of 1.16 (0.56 to 1.76) that Ashok attributes to two early-abstinence studies (Boileau 2008 and 2016) equals the Hedges' g recomputed from Boileau 2016 Table 3 alone; it should not be cited as a pooled two-study estimate.
